intro: In the 1800s, Japan had many small jujutsu schools. Each kept its own lessons on private scrolls. In 1882 a young teacher named Kanō Jigorō opened a school in Tokyo called the Kodokan. He named his subject judo, the gentle way.

Kanō gave judo things the old schools did not share: numbered ranks, a goal of education, and written contest rules. Teachers carried judo into Japanese schools. A world federation formed in 1951, and judo reached the Olympics in Tokyo in 1964.

In this unit you will learn how judo began and how its rulebook works. You will be able to name its ranks, its referee's words and its scores. You will compare its code with boxing's Queensberry Rules of 1867.
bigQuestion: How does a written code turn an old fighting art into a school sport that people everywhere can share?

title: A School with a Rulebook

chapters.title: Kano Writes Judo
chapters.bigQuestion: How did one teacher in Tokyo turn many old fighting schools into a school subject with written ranks and rules?

story.title: Notes on a Temple Desk
story.kicker: In 1882 a young teacher in Tokyo sorts the notes of two old schools into one new plan.
paragraphs: It is 1882 in Tokyo, Japan. Kanō Jigorō is 21 years old. He has just finished his studies at Tokyo University. He rents rooms at Eishōji, a small Buddhist temple in the city.

Kanō has studied jujutsu for years. He trained in two old schools, Tenshin Shin'yō-ryū and Kitō-ryū. Each school kept its own lessons and its own secrets. Each teacher passed them to a few chosen students.
Kanō wants something different. He wants lessons that any student can learn in order. He wants a name, a plan and ranks that anyone can read. He calls his new school the Kodokan and his subject judo.
Only a few students come at first. The room is small and the mats are few. But Kanō keeps writing and teaching. Within a few years, schools and police across Japan know the Kodokan's name.
story.think: Why might a teacher want lessons written down in order instead of kept secret?

lessons.title: Many Old Schools
lessons.mainIdea: Before judo, Japan had many separate jujutsu schools, each called a ryū.
reading: In Japan from the 1600s to the 1800s, many teachers taught *jujutsu*. The word means the gentle art or the soft skill. It was a set of ways to handle an attacker without a weapon, or with a small one.

Each teaching family was called a *ryū*, which means a school or a stream. A ryū had its own name, founder and lessons. Records list many different jujutsu ryū in this long era, called the Edo period.
A ryū often gave written scrolls to its best students. These scrolls named the lessons and the teachers before them. The scrolls were private. Outsiders could not easily read them or join.

words.d: old Japanese arts of handling an attacker without a weapon; the word means soft skill
a Japanese teaching school or family line with its own name and lessons

lessons.title: When the Samurai Class Ended
lessons.mainIdea: After 1868, Japan's new government ended the samurai class, and many jujutsu schools lost students.
reading: In 1868 a new government took power in Japan. This change is called the *Meiji Restoration*. The new leaders wanted railways, factories, an army like Europe's and public schools for all children.
The new government ended the old ranks of society. The samurai, a warrior class, lost their special place. In 1876 a law banned most people from wearing swords in public.
Many old arts looked out of date in this fast new Japan. Some jujutsu teachers lost their students and their pay. Some performed for money. Some ryū closed, and their lessons were nearly lost.

lessons.title: A Young Student Looks for Teachers
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō Jigorō, born in 1860, studied jujutsu with teachers from two old schools.
reading: *Kanō Jigorō* was born in 1860 in Mikage, near Kobe, Japan. His family moved to Tokyo when he was a boy. He was a strong student in English and other school subjects.
As a teenager, Kanō wanted to study jujutsu. He found a teacher named Fukuda Hachinosuke of the Tenshin Shin'yō-ryū. After Fukuda died, he trained with Iso Masatomo of the same school.
Later Kanō trained with Iikubo Tsunetoshi of the *Kitō-ryū*. Now he knew the lessons of two different schools. He began to compare them and keep what he thought worked best for students.

lessons.title: Eishōji Temple, 1882
lessons.mainIdea: In 1882 Kanō opened the Kodokan at a Tokyo temple and named his subject judo.
reading: In 1882 Kanō opened a training room at *Eishōji*, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. It had only a few mats. He called his school the *Kodokan*. The name means a place for teaching the way.
Kanō named his subject judo, the gentle way. The word ju is the same one in jujutsu. Do means a way or path. Kanō chose do to show that judo was a way of living and learning, not only fighting.
The school moved several times as it grew. It needed bigger rooms for more students. Today the Kodokan Judo Institute stands in the Bunkyō area of Tokyo, and it still keeps judo's official ranks.

lessons.title: Judo as Education
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō said judo should train the body, the mind and good character, like a school subject.
reading: Kanō was a teacher first. In 1889 he gave a talk in Tokyo on judo and education. He said judo could train three things: the body, skill in contests, and the mind and character.

In 1922 Kanō began the Kodokan Culture Society. He used two short phrases to sum up judo. *Seiryoku zen'yō* means best use of energy. *Jita kyōei* means mutual welfare and benefit, or you and others doing well together.
These ideas made judo sound like a school subject. Parents and schools could see a goal beyond winning. Kanō wanted students to use judo lessons in study, work and daily life.

look.title: Kanō on Three Goals

lessons.title: Ranks Anyone Can Read
lessons.mainIdea: The Kodokan used numbered kyū and dan ranks, and the black belt became the sign of dan rank.
reading: Old ryū often marked progress with private scrolls. Kanō used numbered ranks instead. Beginners held *kyū* grades. Advanced students held *dan* grades, counted first dan, second dan and up.
In 1883 Kanō gave the first dan grades. Two of the first were his students Saigō Shirō and Tomita Tsunejirō. Over time, a black belt became the visible sign that a student held a dan rank.
A number is easy to read. A student from one judo club could tell another club what rank they held. The Kodokan kept records of each promotion. This made ranks public, not secret.

lessons.title: Teaching the Teachers
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō led a school that trained teachers, which helped carry judo into Japan's schools.
reading: Kanō worked in education for most of his life. For many years he was the head of the Tokyo Higher Normal School. A *normal school* is a college that trains new teachers.

Teachers trained there went on to schools across Japan. In the early 1900s, Japanese middle schools began to offer judo and kendo, the sword art, as school subjects. Judo now had a place in the school timetable.

Kanō also looked beyond Japan. In 1909 he became the first member from Asia on the International Olympic Committee, called the IOC. He traveled to Europe and the United States many times to speak about judo.

lessons.title: A World Judo Body
lessons.mainIdea: In 1951 national judo groups formed the International Judo Federation to share one set of rules.
reading: Kanō died in 1938, on a ship coming home from an IOC meeting in Cairo, Egypt. By then judo clubs met in Britain, France and elsewhere in Europe, the Americas and other parts of Asia.

After World War II, national judo groups wanted to hold contests together. In 1951 they formed the *International Judo Federation*, or IJF. A *federation* is a group of member groups that agree on shared rules.
The IJF set rules for world contests. It ran the first World Judo Championships in Tokyo in 1956. The Kodokan still kept ranks in Japan, while the IJF ran world events.

lessons.title: Tokyo 1964
lessons.mainIdea: Judo first became an Olympic sport at the 1964 Tokyo Games, where Anton Geesink won the open class.
reading: Tokyo hosted the Summer Olympics in 1964. Judo was on the program for the first time. The contests were held in the *Nippon Budokan*, a new hall built in Tokyo for martial arts.

There were four events, all for men. Three had *weight classes*, groups of athletes of similar body weight. The fourth was an open class for any weight. Japanese athletes won the three weight-class gold medals.
The open class ended in a surprise. Anton Geesink of the Netherlands beat Kaminaga Akio of Japan for the gold. His win showed that judo now belonged to athletes from many countries.

reading: Kanō taught some women judo privately in the early 1900s. In 1926 the Kodokan opened a women's section. Women trained there, but for decades they had few official contests.

*Keiko Fukuda* trained at that women's section in the 1930s. She was the granddaughter of Fukuda Hachinosuke, Kanō's first teacher. She later taught judo in California for many years, and USA Judo named her tenth dan in 2011.
Judo joined the *Paralympic Games* in Seoul in 1988. Paralympic judo is for athletes who are blind or have low vision. Women's judo became an Olympic medal sport in 1992 in Barcelona.

chapters.title: Why a Code Matters
chapters.bigQuestion: How does a written rulebook turn a contest into a school sport that strangers in many countries can share?

story.title: The Page Says Begin
story.kicker: Two athletes in white and blue wait at the edge of a mat until a rule lets them start.
paragraphs: A judo hall is full and quiet. Two athletes stand at the edge of a square of mats. One wears a white jacket. One wears a blue jacket. They come from different countries and speak different languages.

Neither athlete steps onto the mat yet. The International Judo Federation's rules say how a contest opens. The athletes walk to their marks. They bow to each other, a standing bow the rules call for at the start of every contest.

Then the referee says one Japanese word: hajime. It means begin. A clock starts. Three officials watch. Every score, penalty and stop will follow the same written rules used in Paris, Tokyo or Rio de Janeiro.
When the contest ends, the two athletes return to their marks and bow again. The rulebook gave the contest a start, an end and a way to name the winner. That page is older than either of them.
story.think: What would change if each country used its own rules for this contest?

lessons.title: Three Ways to Practice
lessons.mainIdea: Kodokan judo named three kinds of practice: set forms, free practice and the contest.
reading: Kanō's Kodokan used named kinds of practice. *Kata* are set forms. Two partners follow a fixed order of named movements, like a written piece of music. Kata kept older lessons from being lost.
*Randori* means free practice. Partners practice with each other without a set order, and no one keeps score. Kanō thought randori and kata worked best together.
*Shiai* means contest. A shiai has a winner and a loser, so it needs clear rules. Who may enter? When does it start? What counts as a score? The contest is where judo needed a written code most.

words.d: a set form: a fixed order of named movements practiced by partners
free practice in judo, with no set order and no score
a judo contest with rules, officials and a winner

lessons.title: A Contest Code on Paper
lessons.mainIdea: Around 1900 the Kodokan wrote contest rules, and in 1951 the IJF began world rules.
reading: In judo's early years, many contests were held between Kodokan students and students of older jujutsu schools. Each side could argue about what was fair. Written rules helped settle those arguments before a match began.

Around 1900 the Kodokan wrote down its own contest rules. The rules named how a match was scored and which moves were not allowed. The Dai Nippon Butokukai, a national martial arts body founded in Kyoto in 1895, also worked on shared rules.

After the International Judo Federation formed in 1951, it wrote the rules for world contests. The IJF still updates its *refereeing rules*, usually every few years. A club in Illinois and a club in Japan can read the same rules.

words.d: a national Japanese martial arts body founded in Kyoto in 1895
the written rules officials use to run a contest and name the winner

lessons.title: Words the Referee Says
lessons.mainIdea: Judo referees around the world call out the same Japanese words to start and stop a contest.
reading: In a judo contest, the *referee* is the official on the mat who runs the match. The referee uses Japanese words everywhere, from Brazil to Canada. The words came from the Kodokan's Tokyo rooms.
*Hajime* means begin. The referee says it to start the contest. *Matte* means wait. The referee says it to pause the match, for example when athletes go off the mat area.
Sore made means that is all. The referee says it when time runs out. Keeping these words in Japanese lets athletes who share no language still understand every call.

a Japanese word meaning begin; the referee's call to start a judo contest

lessons.title: Ippon Ends the Match
lessons.mainIdea: In judo, an ippon is a full point that ends the contest at once.
reading: Judo rules name different scores. The highest is *ippon*, which means one full point. When a referee calls ippon, the contest ends right away, even if time is left on the clock.
A smaller score is called *waza-ari*. The IJF rules have changed how waza-ari counts several times. The rules also removed a smaller score called yuko in 2017, to make scoring simpler to follow.
Senior IJF contests today last four minutes. If the score is tied when time runs out, the contest goes to golden score. In golden score, the first athlete to score wins.

lessons.title: Sorting by Weight
lessons.mainIdea: Weight classes let athletes compete against others of similar size, and their number has changed over time.
reading: Early judo contests in Japan often did not sort athletes by weight. A small athlete could face a much larger one. Kanō taught that skill could overcome size, and stories of small winners were told proudly.
Modern contest rules use weight classes for fairness and safety. At the 1964 Olympics, men's judo had three weight classes and an open class. The number of events grew in the years after.

The open class was dropped from the Olympics after 1984. Since 2000, Olympic judo has had seven weight classes for men and seven for women. Each class has a set top weight, weighed before the contest.

lessons.title: Penalties and Fair Play
lessons.mainIdea: Judo rules name penalties, from a small shido to a hansoku-make that ends the contest.
reading: A rulebook does more than list scores. It also says what is not allowed. Judo rules have always named some moves as banned in contests, because they are too dangerous. Referees stop a contest when one is tried.
A small penalty is called *shido*, which means guidance. A referee may give shido when an athlete avoids contact or steps out of the contest area. Too many shido can cost an athlete the match.

The biggest penalty is *hansoku-make*, which means defeat by a serious rule break. It ends the contest. An athlete can also be given hansoku-make for acting against the spirit of judo, such as disrespect.

words.d: a small penalty in judo; the word means guidance
the biggest judo penalty, which ends the contest with a loss
a punishment in a contest for breaking a rule

look.title: Two Kinds of Rule
look.text: Rule A says what earns a point. Rule B says what is not allowed and what happens if someone does it anyway. A contest needs both kinds to be fair.
look.prompt: What might go wrong if a rulebook had only Rule A?

check.q: What does shido mean?
check.why: Shido means guidance and is a small penalty.

check.q: What does hansoku-make do?
choices: ends the contest with a loss for the rule-breaker
check.why: Hansoku-make is the biggest penalty and ends the contest.

check.q: Why do judo rules ban some moves in contests?
check.why: Some moves are banned in contests for safety.

lessons.title: The Bow at the Edge
lessons.mainIdea: Judo rules and many judo clubs include a bow, called rei, at the start and end of practice and contests.
reading: In Japan, people bow as an everyday greeting and a sign of respect. Kanō's Kodokan made the bow part of judo practice. The Japanese word for a bow is *rei*.

The IJF rules say athletes bow to each other at the start and end of a contest. Many judo clubs also ask students to bow when they step onto or off the mat. Clubs describe it as a sign of respect for partners and the room.
In judo, the bow is a greeting, not worship. The *dojo*, or practice hall, may also be a school gym or a rented room. Clubs around the world keep this Kodokan custom.

words.d: the Japanese word for a bow, used in judo as a greeting and sign of respect
a practice hall for a Japanese martial art; the word means place of the way

look.title: Two Starting Signals
look.text: At a basketball game, players shake hands and the referee tosses the ball up. At a judo contest, athletes bow to each other, and the referee says hajime. Both rooms have a set start.
look.prompt: What does each starting signal tell the players?

check.q: What is rei?
check.why: Rei is the Japanese word for a bow.

check.q: What do judo clubs say the bow shows?
choices: respect for partners and the room
check.why: Clubs describe the bow as a greeting and sign of respect.

check.q: When do IJF rules call for a bow?
choices: at the start and end of a contest
check.why: IJF rules call for a bow at the start and end of each contest.

lessons.title: An English Code, 1867
lessons.mainIdea: The 1867 Queensberry Rules did for boxing what Kodokan rules later did for judo: they put the contest on paper.
reading: Fifteen years before the Kodokan opened, boxing got a written code in England. The *Queensberry Rules* were published in 1867. John Graham Chambers wrote them, and the Marquess of Queensberry gave them his name.
The rules called for a ring 24 feet across, rounds of three minutes and padded gloves. A boxer who went down had ten seconds to get up. The Marquess was a Scottish nobleman, John Sholto Douglas.
Judo and boxing grew in different lands and have different rules. But both codes did the same big job. They wrote down a start, an end, what was banned and how a winner was named.

words.d: boxing's written rules of 1867, named for the Marquess of Queensberry
a written set of rules that everyone in a sport agrees to follow

look.title: From the Queensberry Rules
look.text: The rounds are three minutes long, with one minute of rest between them. The boxers wear fair-sized gloves of good quality. A boxer who falls gets ten seconds to stand up; if not, the other boxer wins.
look.cite: The Queensberry Rules (London Amateur Athletic Club, drafted by John Graham Chambers), 1867
look.prompt: Which of these rules is like a judo rule you read about?

check.q: When were the Queensberry Rules published?
check.why: The Queensberry Rules came out in 1867.

check.q: Who wrote the Queensberry Rules?
check.why: John Graham Chambers wrote them; the Marquess gave his name.

check.q: What job did both the Queensberry Rules and judo's rules do?
choices: They wrote down a start, an end and how to name a winner
check.why: Both codes put the contest's start, end and scoring on paper.

lessons.title: Rules That Keep Changing
lessons.mainIdea: Judo's code keeps changing, from blue jackets in the 1990s to a mixed team event in 2021.
reading: For most of judo's history, both athletes wore white. Referees and viewers could mix them up. In the late 1990s, the IJF began using one blue jacket and one white jacket in top contests.
Rule changes also add new events. At the Tokyo Olympics, held in 2021, judo added a *mixed team* event. Each team had both men and women from one country.

Some people in judo argued against changes like the blue jacket. They said white was part of Kanō's tradition. The IJF decided that clear viewing mattered more. A living code is argued over and rewritten.

words.d: the jacket and trousers worn for judo
an event where each country's team includes both men and women

look.title: White Versus Blue
look.text: Photo one: two athletes in white jackets on a white-lit mat. It is hard to tell who is who. Photo two: one athlete in white and one in blue. A viewer far away can follow each athlete.
look.prompt: Who gains from the blue jacket? Who might miss the all-white look?

check.why: One blue and one white jacket make athletes easier to tell apart.

check.q: What is a mixed team event?

check.why: A mixed team has both men and women from one country.

check.q: Why did some people argue against the blue jacket?
choices: they felt white was part of Kanō's tradition
check.why: Some said the white jacket was part of judo's tradition.
